items.title: Fluid-Gen-Zero: Grounding Pretrained Video Generators in Physics without Training
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Fluid-Gen-Zero, a training-free framework for physics-aware fluid-object interaction video generation that decouples physical reasoning from appearance synthesis. Our key insight is to delegate motion dynamics to a physics simulator while preserving the appearance modeling capacity of pretrained video generators. We bridge these two domains through a two-level agentic workflow: generation-time planning, where a vision-language model (VLM) agent interprets intent and the simulation rollout to organize generation clips, and latent-space guidance, which injects simulation signals into denoising through region-aware latent wrapping. This plug-and-play design is compatible with current video foundation models. We further introduce a benchmark for fluid-object interaction video generation. Across Tora (CogVideoX-based), VACE and WanMove (Wan-based), Fluid-Gen-Zero consistently improves simulation alignment, reducing object trajectory error by 26.7%-81.5% and fluid fEPE (fluid flow endpoint error) by 67.9%-84.0%, while largely preserving perceptual quality. In a human preference study, raters favor Fluid-Gen-Zero in 55.1%-74.4% of same-backbone comparisons across three backbones, and in 90.4%-94.2% of comparisons against simulation-based methods. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: IntactWorld: Joint World Modeling with Intact Features
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While recent video generation models synthesize highly realistic visuals, they lack a genuine understanding of intrinsic real-world logic. Existing methods attempt to understand the world by internalizing diverse world knowledge, yet constrained by computational overhead or dimensionality alignment, their learning processes inevitably compress features, causing a severe loss of structural information. To address this, we propose \textbf{IntactWorld}, a \textbf{Joint World Modeling Architecture} utilizing uncompressed \textbf{Intact Features}. Since data naturally reside on a low-dimensional manifold within a high-dimensional space, predicting the flow velocity $v$ within this uncompressed high-dimensional space induces a severe manifold gap. To successfully eliminate this optimization bottleneck, our framework instead predicts the clean feature $x_0$ at intermediate layers. Furthermore, to mitigate the computational overhead of incorporating complete world knowledge, we introduce a \textit{Full-to-Compact Training Paradigm}. By replacing raw full features with highly refined CLS tokens, this paradigm enables efficient single-branch guidance, reducing spatial memory consumption by 11.4\% and cutting inference latency by 43.8\%. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of IntactWorld, outperforming established baselines by 2.46 points on the VBench 2.0 benchmark.

items.title: Breaking the Group Size Barrier: Parameter-Efficient Group Dance Generation with Chain-of-Dancers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Group dance generation aims to synthesize coordinated multi-dancer choreography from music, with broad applications in animation and interactive content creation. This task requires modeling dense inter-person dependencies to ensure spatial coordination, while naturally preserving individual dancer identities. Existing approaches model all dancers jointly with end-to-end transformers, which tie the architecture to a fixed group size and entangle per-dancer identities across frames. We propose ChainDance, a scalable framework that reformulates group dance generation as a Chain-of-Dancers: a sequential decomposition over per-dancer conditional distributions, allowing a single model to scale across variable group sizes without retraining and naturally preserving per-dancer identity. Built on a frozen single-dancer diffusion backbone, ChainDance introduces two lightweight modules: a Role-Aware Text Encoder (RATE) for per-dancer semantic conditioning, and a Group-Aware Motion Encoder (GAME) that aggregates previously generated dancers via a distance-weighted graph convolutional network, and incorporates a training-free noise optimization procedure at inference time to enforce global spatial coherence. Experiments on AIOZ-GDance demonstrate that ChainDance achieves state-of-the-art motion quality and group coordination while structurally preserving per-dancer identity, with $3$-$4\times$ fewer parameters and requiring $3$-$6\times$ less training time compared to prior approaches.

items.title: When Scene Text Hijacks the Scene: Uncovering, Exploiting, and Mitigating Rendered-Text Semantic Leakage in Image Generation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reliability and accountability of image generative models (IGMs) are essential for building responsible and trustworthy AI systems. Recent IGMs, such as Nano Banana and GPT-Image, now support complex instruction following, realistic image synthesis, and controllable scene-text rendering. As these capabilities expand, safety analysis must also account for new control channels introduced by complex prompts. In this work, we study rendered-text semantic leakage, a largely overlooked phenomenon in open-domain text rendering. Although rendered text is intended to serve as a local visual constraint that should be reproduced verbatim in the generated image, it also carries linguistic semantics that may be interpreted by the model as part of the input instruction. This makes rendered text a potential semantic control channel whose safety implications remain insufficiently understood. We systematically characterize this phenomenon by decoupling the main visual prompt from the rendered text and measuring their individual and compositional effects on generated images. We quantify semantic leakage and rendering fidelity, and further analyze how leakage emerges from intermediate model evidence. We then show that harmful semantics embedded in scene text can persist through LLM-based prompt enhancement pipelines and steer non-text image regions, even when the main visual prompt remains benign. Finally, we propose a preliminary mitigation approach that reduces unsafe semantic transfer from rendered text to non-text regions while preserving the intended text-rendering behavior on FLUX-2-dev. Our findings reveal rendered text as a dual-use carrier of visible data and latent semantics, exposing a text-centric cross-modal attack surface in modern IGMs.

items.title: iCATS: Fast Video Generation via Interaction-Aware Sparse Attention and Timestep-Adaptive Sparsity
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training-free sparse attention offers a practical acceleration solution to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) via reducing computations without fine-tuning. It typically involves estimating the importance of query-key regions and deriving sparse masks to compute only the important candidates, which inevitably introduces approximation errors that may degrade generation quality. To better balance the efficiency-quality trade-off, we propose iCATS, integrating improved importance estimation and sparse mask construction with an efficient hardware execution strategy. Specifically, for importance estimation, unlike previous works that perform independent clustering over query and key tokens based on feature similarity to estimate attention scores, iCATS demonstrates that clustering based on query-key dot-product interactions is more accurate and further reformulates this objective as a simple quadratic form for low-cost computation. For sparse mask construction, instead of using a fixed top-p rule, we observe that tolerance to sparse approximation errors varies across denoising timesteps and therefore introduce an SNR-guided sparsity schedule to adjust sparsity dynamically, leading to higher accuracy. Finally, for hardware execution, we devise a tail-merging strategy to reduce padding overhead caused by irregular cluster sizes, improving GPU kernel utilization. Extensive experiments show that iCATS achieves $2.03\times$ acceleration with 31.017 dB PSNR on HunyuanVideo-T2V-13B and $1.55\times$ acceleration with 29.301 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B, delivering a state-of-the-art efficiency-quality trade-off.

items.title: PathLang: A Language-Centered Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Computational Pathology
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pathology vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong visual perception ability, but their robustness in the language domain remains poorly characterized. Existing pathology VLM benchmarks largely rely on canonical closed-set prompts or perturb only generic templates, treating language as a fixed evaluation component rather than a variable axis of model behavior. In clinical practice, however, diagnostic language varies across reports, institutions, and candidate diagnoses. We introduce PathLang, a language-centered and clinically grounded zero-shot benchmark. PathLang holds the underlying slides, ground-truth labels, and image-text evaluation direction fixed while systematically varying only the diagnostic language, so that performance differences reflect how a diagnosis is phrased rather than what is imaged. The language variation follows how pathologists actually rephrase diagnoses (terminology, specificity, and reporting style), and all prompts and candidate pools are validated by six board-certified pathologists. PathLang covers four task families: (1) zero-shot classification with image-text alignment analysis, (2) cross-modal retrieval, (3) paraphrase robustness, including semantic-equivalence paraphrases, length and reporting-style variation, and prompt ensembling, and (4) open-vocabulary diagnosis retrieval over four candidate pools with distinct forms of semantic competition. Across nine VLMs and five public datasets spanning four organs, we find that performance is highly sensitive to clinically equivalent paraphrases, varies substantially across forms of semantic competition, and that image-text alignment quality does not necessarily translate into inter-class separability. We release the prompt corpus, candidate pools, pre-computed text embeddings, and evaluation code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PathLang.

items.title: Sony’s New Spatial Audio USB-C Mic Aims to Bring a New Level of Immersion to Content Creators
items.summary: The new era of immersive content is coming, or, in some ways, already here. The question is more about timing than anything else at this point, so if you want to get ahead, now might be a good time to start exploring these new workflows. To help with this, Sony has unveiled its new ECM-AX10 spatial audio USB-C microphone, which features four omnidirectional electret condenser capsules, making it capable of recording everything from stereo and binaural audio to full ambisonics. Is it overkill for most content creators? Maybe a little, but it's cool and worth exploring for the future, maybe a bit too. Let’s check it out. The New Sony ECM-AX10 The Sony ECM-AX10 aims to deliver immersive audio that matches the content and video recorded by high-end pros, while also serving everyday creators looking to capture content or even go live. The Sony ECM-AX10 features a built-in accelerometer that auto-detects the microphone’s orientation and adjusts accordingly, helping it handle all the audio situations listed above, from stereo to ambisonic. The mic also offers a range of other audio-recording workflow features, including switchable noise-cut and low-cut filters, auto gain control, and a dedicated ATT switch. It even has a dedicated SELFIE switch that can adjust sound orientation for front-facing video, if that’s what you’re into. Price and Availability The Sony ECM-AX10 aims to deliver a lot with its immersive upside, but it’s also a regular microphone with a 3.5mm headphone output that should enable direct, zero-latency monitoring and your usual mix of mic bells and whistles. If you’d like to learn more about this option and explore its advanced spatial audio processing in more detail, here are the full specs and purchase options. items.title: The Most Instantly Recognizable Film Scores of All Time
items.summary: Everybody loves a good musical score for a movie. When utilized properly, they elevate the desired emotions performed by the actors and can also accentuate the gravity of a moment when properly restrained. But it’s the movies that you simply cannot imagine without the music in front of them that truly stand the test of time. Let’s talk about some of those. Star Wars I’ve got to get the granddaddy of them all out of the way somewhere. The original Star Wars film from 1977 is one of the most miraculously conceived projects ever to grace the silver screen. And when you do the unthinkable and remove John Williams’ score from any given moment, it’s abundantly clear that at least 75 percent, if not far more, of the film’s success can be directly attributed to how the score interacts with all of the visuals. This is not meant to diminish the other accomplishments of the film, but when you actually take a step back and look at how aggressively the medium shifted after Star Wars was released, if it had a different score, the cinematic landscape today would probably look a lot different. Also, in the interest of diversity and keeping this listicle interesting to read, this is going to be the only John Williams score we talk about today. If I didn’t implement this rule, the artist distribution rate just wouldn’t be fair. Psycho ‘Psycho’Credit: Universal Pictures One of the most underrated composers of the 60s and 70s is Bernard Herrmann. He collaborated frequently with Alfred Hitchcock on his other films like Vertigo and North by Northwest, as well as with Martin Scorsese for the beautifully hypnotic compositions for Taxi Driver. However, his most instantly recognizable track is undeniably the ear-piercing violin strings from Hitchcock’s masterpiece, Psycho. And it almost didn’t happen that way at all. items.title: Parametric Trajectory Distillation for Few-Step Video Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video diffusion and flow models require many sequential evaluations, making generation computationally expensive. Few-step distillation reduces this cost but poses a capacity allocation problem: a student must match the teacher's iterative generation with far less sequential computation. Existing trajectory methods ask the student to reproduce teacher transitions that are highly curved at high noise, which can exceed its capacity and degrade fine detail. We introduce Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD), which lets the student parameterize teacher trajectory segments as polynomials and learn from teacher guidance along its own predicted path. PTD is designed to let the learned curvature adapt to the backbone's predictive capacity, preserving motion and diversity. The curvature head is used only in training; inference keeps the original backbone architecture. On Wan2.1-14B, four-step PTD sets a new state of the art for trajectory distillation, significantly improving dynamic quality and naturalness over PDD, the best-performing trajectory-only method on this model, under the same training setting. On the 33B audio-video MiniMax-H3, LoRA-trained PTD significantly improves diversity and naturalness over the state-of-the-art LightX2V Turbo. Blinded human votes give PTD 55.1% and 63.4% preference shares against PDD and LightX2V Turbo. Project page: https://alan-lanfeng.github.io/PTD/.

items.title: All In on AI? This New NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X-Powered Laptop Could Be For You
items.summary: We know it’s not for everyone, but the AI market is growing. Or at least that’s what the market is telling us, as new products and machines tailored specifically for these new types of developers and creators keep coming out. The new Lenovo 15.3" Pro 9n Multi-Touch Laptop is a perfect example of a highly ambitious (and highly expensive) new laptop that is built specifically for creators and developers whose work demands substantial local computing capabilities. Powered by one of NVIDIA’s latest superchips (the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X), this new Lenovo laptop aims to be an all-in AI machine, if that’s something you’re into, of course. The Lenovo 15.3" Pro 9n Multi-Touch Laptop The big selling point for this new Lenovo laptop, and what makes it worth its $3,000+ price point, is the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip at its heart. This RTX Spark N1X is further boosted by an NVIDIA Grace 18-Core CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX 5120-Core GPU, and 32GB of unified LPDDR5x RAM, delivering top-end performance tailored for… you guessed it… high-end AI work. What’s unique about this Pro 9n model is that it does offer a nice mix of AI-prioritized features like its advanced local workloads, substantial unified memory, and RTX capabilities, but still a portable design so you can use all of its AI inference, 3D rendering, and creative workloads from wherever your work may take you. Price and Availability If AI isn't your thing, that’s understandable. It’s also understandable if this isn't the laptop for you. items.title: Expression-Diverse References for Identity-Preserving Video Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.11023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identity-preserving video generation aims to maintain a subject's identity while synthesizing realistic videos. Yet a single reference portrait captures the subject's appearance under only one facial configuration. As expressions change, facial appearance can vary in highly identity-specific ways, leaving the subject's appearance under unseen expressions underdetermined by the reference alone. This expression-dependent variation also complicates evaluation: similarity to a neutral reference may decrease under strong expressions even for real images of the same person. We investigate this limitation from both generation and evaluation perspectives. First, we quantify how face-recognition similarity varies with expression intensity using controlled photographs and MEAD videos. We then construct a compact yet expressive reference gallery that captures diverse expression-dependent facial configurations. Matching against this gallery provides a more robust measure of identity similarity under expressive motion. To further expose performance degradation with expression intensity, we report identity similarity separately for mild, intense, and extreme expressions. For generation, we extend Stand-In to condition on our expression-diverse reference sets and develop a data-curation pipeline that extracts consistent yet diverse face crops from training videos. In practical settings where only a single portrait is available, we construct the reference set by synthesizing additional expressions with a pretrained facial reenactment model. On our controlled benchmark, both real and synthesized reference sets outperform the evaluated baselines in identity similarity across all three expression-intensity regimes, with the largest improvements for extreme expressions.

items.title: 'Crystal Lake' Premieres October 15: Everything We Know About the Friday the 13th Prequel
items.summary: Crystal Lake, which is the first official installment in the Friday the 13th franchise since 2009, is mere days away from its premiere on Peacock on October 15. The show, which is set to drop all eight episodes of its premiere season on that date, is a prequel following the exploits of Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), the mother of the franchise’s hockey-masked serial killer Jason Voorhees. This will be the franchise’s most thorough exploration of the character of Pamela, who was the killer in the original 1980 Friday the 13th. - YouTube www.youtube.com Who Made Crystal Lake? The production company behind the Peacock series is A24, the independent studio that has had a hand in creating a wide variety of modern cinema’s biggest critical and commercial hits, including Everything Everywhere All At Once, Backrooms, and Moonlight. While they are behind considerably fewer television series than movies, they have contributed a number of notable programs, including HBO’s hit teen drama Euphoria, Netflix’s anthology dramedy Beef, and Prime Video’s coming-of-age comedy Overcompensating. While a Friday the 13th series has been in development hell since the early 2000s, the current incarnation of the series was originally announced in 2022 with Pushing Daisies and Hannibal creator Bryan Fuller at the helm. However, he parted ways from the project in 2024 when A24 opted to go a different direction. Brad Caleb Kane, a writer and executive producer on It: Welcome to Derry and Black Sails (in addition to being the singing voice for Disney’s Aladdin), eventually stepped into the role. The show was shot in New Jersey between June and October 2025, with multiple episodes apiece directed by Michael Lennox (Derry Girls, How to Get to Heaven from Belfast), duo Celine Held and Logan George (Caddo Lake), and Quyen Tran (Ahsoka, The Pitt, The Testaments). items.title: Aaron Sorkin's 6 Biggest Writing Lessons
items.summary: You'd think after, you know, an Oscar, The West Wing, and decades of fast-talking dialogue, writing would get easier for Aaron Sorkin. But it hasn't, according to what he admits in a recent conversation with Esquire editor-in-chief Michael Sebastian. He famously wrote the taut 2010 drama The Social Network. Now he's back with a follow-up. The Social Reckoning hits theaters today, Oct. 9, with Sorkin writing and directing. It tells the true story of Facebook engineer Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), who take on the social network's founder, Mark Zuckerberg (played this time by Jeremy Strong). You can watch the whole interview here, but we've also pulled our favorite bits of advice. - YouTube www.youtube.com Even Sorkin Thinks Every Script Is His Last If you've ever finished a draft and felt completely tapped out, or even like it's maybe the worst thing you've ever done, you're in good company. Sorkin says the struggle never ends. "Writing isn't easy for me. I love it. When I'm done with something, whether it's a movie, a play, or an episode of television, I can't imagine ever being able to write something else. I wrote 88 episodes of The West Wing and 87 times, I said, 'Guys, I'm out. I've used all the words that I know in every order I can put them in. I can't do this.'" He kept going, and his foundation stayed the same. Sorkin has long described his approach in terms of intention and obstacle. Somebody wants something, and something formidable stands in the way. You can keep writing about that until the end of time, in infinite iterations. Burnout is real, and mental health breaks matter. Feeling empty after a project isn't a sign you're done. You just need to step away for a bit, most likely. items.title: Full Frame vs. Super 35 and How Sensor Size Changes Your Shot
items.summary: Few topics start a comment-section fight faster than sensor size. Is your 18mm "really" a 27mm on a crop sensor? Does full frame give you shallower depth of field? Or is that a myth too? If you've ever stood in a rental house trying to decide between a Super 35 body and a full-frame one, the confusion might be real. British filmmaker Woody James clears up the most common confusion in a quick new video. He spent about a decade shooting broadcast documentaries worldwide, with his IMDb credits including Hidden Britain by Drone and The Divide, and now shoots both formats almost daily. Check out the video here. - YouTube www.youtube.com A Primer on Full Frame vs. Super 35 If you're new to cameras, the sensor is the chip inside your camera that captures the image, the digital stand-in for a piece of film. Sensors come in different sizes. Two of the most common in filmmaking are full frame and Super 35. Full frame measures about 36x24mm, modeled on the 35mm still-photo negative. Super 35 is smaller and based on the 35mm motion picture frame, with sizes that vary a bit by manufacturer. For most of film history, cinema cameras shot Super 35. The term "full-frame" took hold once stills cameras like the Canon 5D Mark II started shooting video on their larger sensors. Focal length is a property of the lens, measured in millimeters. Longer focal lengths magnify the scene more. Field of view is how much of the scene ends up in your frame. Depth of field is how much of the image looks sharp from front to back. Crop factor is the number you multiply by to compare framing between sensors. (For Super 35, Canon puts it at about 1.5x.) An 18mm Lens Is Always an 18mm Lens Plenty of filmmakers talk about crop sensors as if they change the lens itself. James says that's backward. "There seems to be a common idea here on YouTube that if, for example, you put an 18 mil lens on a Super 35 mil sensor camera, you should really be describing that lens as a 24 mil. But it's just not true at all.

items.title: Struggling With Framing Up Your Shots? Here’s How to Let Your Sony Cameras Handle it For You
items.summary: What’s been great about the digital camera revolution over the past few years is that it has not only unlocked more cameras for more people to dive into the worlds of photography, videography, and content creation, but it’s also developed new ways to bring accessibility to those who have perhaps never considered any of these avenues in the past due to physical limitations like blindness or low vision. Regardless of why you might want to use a tool like this, Sony’s Auto Frame feature is powerful and can help in a wide range of situations. You just have to understand how to use it. And that’s what this latest feature guide goes over, so let’s dive in. Sony Auto Framing Accessibility Feature Available on most Sony Alpha series cameras, Auto Framing is an accessibility feature that’s super helpful for those who are blind or have low vision, but it's also a sneaky-helpful feature for run-and-gun shooters and solo shooters looking for camera assistance. The Auto Framing feature works pretty much as you’d expect: it helps keep subjects centered in the frame, making it easier to capture content with confidence, even if you can’t fully see what you’re capturing for photo or video. This video is pretty helpful too, as it goes over pretty much everything you need to know about getting started with Auto Framing for the first time, including how to navigate to it in your camera’s settings, as well as explaining how it works, with the cropping frame being able to follow your subject across your screen. More Auto Framing Advice The only other main trick worth mentioning is that this feature works best with wide- to normal-angle lenses, set up to give the camera and sensor enough space and information to track a subject that might move a lot in any direction in the shot. Long lenses and tight close-ups can make this trickier, so keep that in mind when you set up your own cameras and shots, or when you help set up cameras for people with low vision needs. items.title: How ‘Terminator 2’ Created One of Cinema’s Most Realistic Nuclear Explosions With Practical Effects
items.summary: In 1991, director James Cameron built one of cinema's most ambitious practical-effects sequences: a nuclear holocaust that annihilates Los Angeles in Terminator 2: Judgment Day. The sequence was primarily constructed by hand using miniatures, air cannons, matte paintings, and prosthetic body doubles, with digital compositing used to complete specific shots. The result was a sequence that scientists have since cited as one of the most realistic depictions of a nuclear blast ever put on screen. But how did he create one of the most realistic depictions of a nuclear blast? And in 1991? Let’s stop scratching our heads about it and dig in. James Cameron's Vision of a Nuclear Blast The scene takes place in Sarah Connor’s (Linda Hamilton) nightmare premonition, before the main plot starts unfolding. This sequence sets the stakes at the beginning. To heighten the terror, Cameron wanted the scene to feel as real as possible. He wanted to see bodies literally incinerated on screen, along with real destruction and shock waves from the nuclear blast. Gathering the Team and Hatching a Plan 'Terminator 2: Judgment Day' (1991)Credit: Tri-Star Pictures Cameron divided the work across four companies. ILM handled the CGI effects. Stan Winston Studio was responsible for prosthetics and animatronics. Fantasy II Film Effects developed miniatures and optical effects. 4-Ward Productions took on the nuclear explosion sequence specifically. Together, the effects teams studied archival documentary footage of actual nuclear tests to understand the mechanics of the blast wave before building their plan around large-scale miniatures and high-powered air cannons. items.title: Region-Aware CLS Token Augmentation for Fine-Grained Image Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image retrieval methods often rely on a single global semantic descriptor extracted from an image, e.g., the [CLS] token in vision transformers. However, trying to squeeze all the semantic information of an image into a single descriptor can hurt downstream retrieval performance, especially for fine-grained retrieval tasks. In this work, we augment the semantic tokens in the newer visual transformers, the global [CLS] token and the four register tokens, with a carefully selected collection of spatial tokens, aiming to capture the spatial region representation that characterizes the contents captured in each of the semantic tokens. We leverage the DINOv2-reg model, which includes register tokens that emergently learn object and part-based representations. For each "cue" token ([CLS] and each register token), we find a "buddy" image patch token and extract an N x N patch region to produce a set of localized ROI tokens. Our approach automatically captures important regions of interest without any external bounding boxes or saliency modules, purely by matching semantic tokens with their spatial representation regions. Furthermore, we incorporate these tokens into a multi-vector retrieval framework inspired by ColBERT, enabling fine-grained matching via a per-token alignment mechanism while avoiding the large storage cost of keeping all patch embeddings. Through extensive experiments, we find that (1) register tokens encode useful fine-grained details that can complement the [CLS] token; (2) automatically pooled ROI tokens further improve fine-grained discrimination; and (3) multi-vector retrieval with a small set of tokens improves over a DINOv2-reg single-vector baseline while remaining tractable for large-scale search. The code is available at https://github.com/IdhcbIan/Augmenting_CLS_with_ROI_tokens.
